title: ArcFlow: Training Flow Policies for Multiple Solver Budgets

paper.title: ArcFlow : Training Flow Policies for Multiple Solver Budgets
paper.abstract:
Abstract Flow-matching policies adjust inference cost through the number of solver
steps, but reinforcement learning at a single fixed solver budget can hide
degradation at cheaper deployment budgets and even erase useful one-step
behavior present in a pretrained policy. We introduce Action–Ratio–Clip Flow ( ArcFlow ) , a
deployment-aware algorithm for
training one flow policy across a specified range of solver budgets. ArcFlow combines action-aligned supervision, budget exposure, and worst-budget
checkpoint selection. For reconstruction objectives, its bridge aggregates
temporal probes into one surrogate ratio and one PPO-style clip per action,
with a boundary residual exactly equal to deployed one-step reconstruction
error. Cycling exposes the shared field to the deployment range, and selection
optimizes its performance floor. For native velocity objectives, multi-budget
endpoint supervision applies the same principle without replacing the native
update. Both realizations preserve the architecture and deployment-time cost.
Across DM Control, manipulation, and locomotion, ArcFlow attains the highest
mean one-step return among five flow-policy baselines on 25 of
30 tasks under each method’s reported training
settings. Component studies identify complementary improvements from boundary
supervision, the fixed-grid bridge, budget exposure, and deployment selection.
These results establish
deployment-budget-aware training as an effective route to strong low-step
control with one policy serving multiple inference costs. 1 1 1 Code can be accessed at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/arcflow-868A

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Flow matching represents expressive action distributions by learning a velocity field that transports noise to actions ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . Its solver controls inference cost: more steps refine integration, while fewer steps reduce network evaluations, helping robotic policies meet latency budgets. Consistency and shortcut models enable one- and few-step generation ( Song et al., 2023 ; Frans et al., 2025 ) , creating an opportunity to retain expressive policies at low deployment cost. Reinforcement learning (RL) improves policies through interaction. FPO and FPO++ derive policy-gradient surrogates from flow-matching losses ( McAllister et al., 2025 ; Yi et al., 2026 ) ; Diffusion Policy Policy Optimization (DPPO) applies policy gradients to a stochastic diffusion denoising chain ( Ren et al., 2025 ) ; ReinFlow adds learnable exploration noise to flow policies ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) ; and PolicyFlow approximates importance ratios from velocity-field changes along interpolation paths ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . At deployment, solver steps determine latency and may change the action of the same trained field. High return at the training budget gives no assurance of high one-step return; RL can even erode low-step behavior already present in the prior. This gap motivates us to train and select one field across its deployment range (Figure 1 ). Figure 1: ArcFlow for multi-budget deployment. Left: the solver budget K K controls deployment cost. Right: the bridge-based control realization uses fresh noise and the observed action; at the boundary, the residual norm equals one-step reconstruction error. Probes are averaged before one surrogate ratio and PPO clip per action. Rollout budgets cycle, and checkpoint selection maximizes the worst validation return over K ∈ { 1 , 4 , 16 } K\in\{1,4,16\} . Two properties of the training objective and solver discretization help explain this behavior. First, reconstruction-based objectives may provide limited supervision at the deployment boundary. In FPO ( McAllister et al., 2025 ) , for example, the noise-reconstruction formulation weights velocity error by ( 1 − t ) 2 (1-t)^{2} , so the boundary queried by a one-step solver receives zero weight. Direct velocity supervision instead provides a boundary-aligned signal. This observation complements prior work on time-dependent loss weighting in generative modeling ( Choi et al., 2022 ; Hang et al., 2023 ) and highlights the importance of aligning the weighting scheme with the deployed action map. Second, because different solver budgets induce different action maps, updates based on rollouts from a single budget need not improve all budgets uniformly. We study this effect in the ReinFlow ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) fine-tuning pipeline, where native velocity supervision is already available. We introduce Action–Ratio–Clip Flow ( ArcFlow ) , an RL algorithm for one flow field across a specified solver-budget range. Its control realization uses a fixed-grid bridge with an exact one-step action-reconstruction residual. It aggregates temporal probes into one energy-based surrogate ratio and one PPO-style clip per action; the ratio is not the executed policy’s likelihood ratio. For native velocity objectives, multi-budget endpoint losses and an anchored max–min update extend the same deployment principle without replacing the original objective. Both realizations retain one field and the original deployment architecture. Our contributions are: • A diagnosis tied to deployment. We expose one-step degradation hidden by training-budget evaluation and identify how the supervision target suppresses the relevant boundary signal. • An algorithm for multiple solver budgets. We connect an exact action-reconstruction identity to action-aligned supervision, budget exposure, and worst-budget checkpoint selection. • Evidence across objectives and domains. A controlled common-stack benchmark and a released manipulation pipeline test the algorithm, with component studies and deployment-cost accounting identifying the sources of improvement. Across DM Control, manipulation, and locomotion, ArcFlow leads five flow-policy baselines in mean one-step return on 25 of 30 tasks including cross-regime manipulation comparisons.

sections.heading: 2 Problem formulation
sections.text: Let s s denote an environment state, z ∼ p 0 z\sim p_{0} source noise, and v θ ​ ( x , t ∣ s ) v_{\theta}(x,t\mid s) a velocity field with reverse-time convention t : 1 → 0 t:1\to 0 . A numerical solver S K S_{K} with K K steps induces the policy a = F θ S K ​ ( z , s ) a=F^{S_{K}}_{\theta}(z,s) . The environment observes the resulting action; the solver’s internal queries do not constitute environment transitions. Write J K ​ ( θ ) J_{K}(\theta) for the expected episodic return of this policy. Our objective is to learn one field that remains useful across a specified set of deployment budgets, without supplying K K as an input to the field. Flow-policy algorithms use several tractable training signals, including flow-matching residuals, velocity-based surrogates, and likelihoods of stochastic internal transitions. These signals differ in their treatment of solver time. An improvement in a training surrogate, or in J K train J_{K_{\rm train}} , does not in itself imply an improvement in J K J_{K} for a different budget. We distinguish three outcomes. Numerical failure is a non-finite update or evaluation. Cross-budget degradation is a lower return at one deployment budget than another. Temporal degradation is a fall in return during training at a fixed budget. The census calls a task a one-step collapse when its specified one-to-sixteen-step return statistic falls below one half. This threshold is descriptive and depends on the seed pool and aggregation rule; it is not a synonym for temporal degradation. We report the graded return ratio alongside the threshold count.

sections.heading: Collapse versus absolute performance.
sections.text: The collapse count and the mean return capture different aspects of solver-budget behavior. DPPO and PolicyFlow have no marked collapses in Figure 2 (a), yet their mean returns remain well below ArcFlow at every displayed budget in panel (b). Conversely, a method can achieve a higher aggregate return while still containing tasks with severe one-to-sixteen-step degradation. Evaluating low-step return together with within-policy retention is therefore necessary: the absence of collapse alone does not imply an effective low-latency policy.

sections.heading: Common-stack benchmark.
sections.text: We instantiate all methods in a control stack derived from the released FPO Playground configuration. It covers 21 DM Control tasks ( Tassa et al., 2018 ) , 64 outer iterations, and 62.9 62.9 million interactions; fixed-budget arms collect at 4 steps. We compare FPO ( McAllister et al., 2025 ) , FPO++ ( Yi et al., 2026 ) , DPPO ( Ren et al., 2025 ) , ReinFlow ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) , and PolicyFlow ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . All arms share the normalizer, architecture, initialization, critic, and training-interaction budget. The DPPO row applies its denoising-MDP policy-gradient objective to the shared flow actor, not the original diffusion actor; Appendix D specifies the adaptation. Raw returns use each configuration’s registered seeds and display regime; the Panda comparisons are cross-regime. Figure 2 min–max normalizes each task over six methods, five budgets, and a Gaussian reference. “Collapse” means R 1 / R 16 < 0.5 R_{1}/R_{16}<0.5 . The separate can study uses five matched training seeds.

sections.heading: Broad low-budget gains.
sections.text: Table 1 reports the deployed return of all six methods at three deployment budgets on 30 tasks. At K = 1 K=1 , ArcFlow has the highest displayed mean on 25 of 30 tasks under the registered display regimes: 18 of 21 DM Control tasks, all 3 manipulation tasks, and 4 of six locomotion tasks. Across the 25 wins, the strongest baseline is FPO on 11 tasks, PolicyFlow on six, ReinFlow on four, and FPO++ and DPPO on two each. The gains are also often substantial. Using the displayed means, 12 of the 25 wins improve on the strongest baseline by at least 10 % 10\% , and nine improve by at least 20 % 20\% . The largest multiplicative gains occur on HopperStand, where ArcFlow reaches 361 361 versus 115 115 for the strongest baseline; HopperHop, with 60.4 60.4 versus 22.8 22.8 ; and PandaOpenCabinet, with 618 618 versus 225 225 . The advantage is not limited to these outliers: at one step, ArcFlow also obtains 956 956 versus 772 772 on CartpoleBalance, 849 849 versus 672 672 on CheetahRun, 554 554 versus 457 457 on FingerSpin, and 10.5 10.5 versus 7.54 7.54 on Op3Joystick. Thus the lowest-cost setting yields both broad task coverage and pronounced gains on several of the more difficult control and manipulation problems. sections.heading: Domain and budget coverage.
sections.text: The manipulation block provides the clearest uniform result: ArcFlow has the highest displayed mean at all three budgets on PandaPickCube, PandaPickCubeOrient, and PandaOpenCabinet. In DM Control, it is best at all three budgets on eight tasks, including BallInCup, HopperHop, HopperStand, PendulumSwingup, PointMass, ReacherEasy, Swimmer6, and WalkerStand; it also leads all three budgets on Op3Joystick in locomotion. Across the full table, ArcFlow is best on 13 tasks at K = 4 K=4 and 14 at K = 16 K=16 , and on 12 tasks at every reported budget. Task-level leaders are therefore more mixed at higher solver counts than at one step, but the table shows that ArcFlow combines a broad low-budget advantage with strong performance as additional computation becomes available. These task-level counts identify where each method leads; Figure 2 (b) instead shows how each trained field performs as the deployment budget changes, averaged over the 30 tasks. ArcFlow has the highest mean normalized return at every evaluated solver count, with the largest separation at one step. Its mean rises from one to two steps and then remains nearly constant through sixteen steps. Figure 2 (a) likewise records no one-step collapse for ArcFlow across the 30-task census. Although the strongest high-budget method varies on the remaining tasks, the aggregate curve stays above all baselines. sections.heading: Early emergence of low-step gains.
sections.text: Figure 3 shows that the deployed advantage often emerges before training ends. On CheetahRun, FingerSpin, HopperHop, HopperStand, the Walker tasks, and the manipulation tasks, ArcFlow separates from most baselines by roughly mid-training. Its Hopper returns rise steadily while competing curves remain near the floor or plateau lower, so Table 1 ’s differences are not created solely by the deployed endpoints.

sections.heading: Stable and late-stage improvement.
sections.text: On BallInCup, PointMass, ReacherEasy, and ReacherHard, ArcFlow rises early and remains stable; PendulumSwingup, Swimmer6, H1JoystickGait, and Op3Joystick keep improving after mid-training. On CartpoleBalance, PandaOpenCabinet, and H1InplaceGait, the selected rightmost marker rises above the preceding chronological trajectory. The deployed result thus combines early acquisition, continued gains, and checkpoint selection.

sections.heading: 5.5 Native-pipeline validation
sections.text: Table 5.2 tests whether the same deployment-budget principle transfers beyond the reconstruction-based control realization. The released ReinFlow ShortCut pipeline starts from a behavior-cloned image policy, uses native velocity supervision, and fine-tunes a four-step actor. It tests the principle beyond FPO’s reconstruction target and compares one multi-budget policy with a one-step specialist and rollout-budget cycling. The released behavior-cloned prior retains moderate performance across solver budgets, but official ReinFlow fine-tuning raises four-step success to 92.5 92.5 % while reducing one-step success to 1.5 1.5 %. The specialist reverses this tradeoff: it reaches 98.0 98.0 % at one step but has a worst-budget score of only 74.6 74.6 %. Cycling performs best at two and four steps, yet falls to 78.3 78.3 % at its weakest budget. In contrast, ArcFlow remains between 91.1 91.1 % and 97.1 97.1 % across all five budgets, giving the highest worst-budget score ( 91.1 91.1 %) and mean score ( 94.7 94.7 %). Thus, its advantage is the high performance floor obtained with one field across the deployment range.

sections.heading: 6 Related work
sections.text: Generative transport and control. Diffusion models learn reverse transport from noise to data ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ) , while deterministic samplers and neural ODEs expose an accuracy–computation tradeoff ( Song et al., 2021a ; Chen et al., 2018 ) . Flow matching and rectified flow learn velocity fields directly ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) ; transport couplings and multisample matching straighten paths, and rectified flows scale to high-resolution generation ( Tong et al., 2024 ; Pooladian et al., 2023 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . In control, generative models support planning and return conditioning ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Ajay et al., 2023 ) , plus visuomotor imitation across 2D, goal-conditioned, and 3D inputs ( Chi et al., 2023 ; Reuss et al., 2023 ; Ze et al., 2024 ) . AdaFlow adapts integration to action variance and FlowPolicy learns one-step consistency ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . This work instead trains one flow field with RL for a declared set of deployment budgets. Reinforcement learning of generative policies. Trust-region and clipped policy objectives motivate many modern policy updates ( Schulman et al., 2015 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ) . DDPO casts denoising as an MDP, while DRaFT differentiates rewards through the sampler ( Black et al., 2024 ; Clark et al., 2024 ) . For control, DPPO applies policy gradients to diffusion-policy denoising transitions and QVPO uses a value-weighted update ( Ren et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2024 ) . ReinFlow makes flow transitions stochastic; FPO and FPO++ form PPO-style ratios from flow losses; PolicyFlow and Flow-GRPO derive velocity- or transition-based objectives ( Zhang et al., 2025b ; McAllister et al., 2025 ; Yi et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . Offline and critic-based methods include Diffusion-QL, EDP, DTQL, BDPO, Q-score matching, Flow Q-Learning, and SAC Flow ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Kang et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Psenka et al., 2024 ; Park et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . ArcFlow focuses on the return floor of one policy across solver budgets. Few-step and one-step policies. DDIM and DPM-Solver accelerate sampling numerically ( Song et al., 2021a ; Lu et al., 2022 ) ; progressive distillation, consistency models, and InstaFlow learn fast generators ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . Shortcut models and MeanFlow train directly over variable or one-step generation ( Frans et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) , and Consistency Policy distills a visuomotor policy ( Prasad et al., 2024 ) . One-step flow policy mirror descent, FLAME, and MFPO bring this objective to RL ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026 ) . These methods optimize a designated short sampler or fast policy; ArcFlow preserves one RL-trained field and measures it at every declared K ∈ 𝒦 K\in\mathcal{K} . Training-time weighting and deployment budgets. P2, Min-SNR, and EDM reweight diffusion times ( Choi et al., 2022 ; Hang et al., 2023 ; Karras et al., 2022 ) . Our problematic weight instead follows algebraically from noise reconstruction and is zero at the one-step boundary. Boundary supervision restores that signal, solver cycling exposes the intended budgets, and worst-budget selection makes their return floor an explicit selection criterion.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: ArcFlow aligns flow-policy learning with its deployment range through boundary supervision, solver-budget exposure, and worst-budget selection. Across three control domains it improves one-step performance while retaining competitive higher-budget returns; the native ReinFlow study extends the principle to a released image-policy pipeline and five budgets. Deployment retains one architecture and pays only for the selected solver budget. Component studies further separate the gains from action-aligned supervision, budget exposure, and selection. These results support training and evaluating generative policies over their full deployment range.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: Generative AI tools were used to help develop and critique the conceptual framework and hypotheses; formulate mathematical claims and proofs; design synthetic environments and experimental protocols; implement, test, and edit software; interpret results; search literature; prepare figures and tables; and draft and edit the manuscript. AI-generated outputs were not treated as empirical evidence: reported values come from versioned artifacts, citations are checked against primary sources, and assumptions and proofs are stated in the paper. Generative AI was not used to generate or clean experimental datasets or to translate source material; qualitative or thematic data analysis was not applicable. We reviewed the AI-assisted work and take responsibility for the final text, claims, code, and artifacts.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: This work studies reinforcement learning for simulated control and does not involve human participants, personal data, or physical-robot experiments. Like other reinforcement-learning methods, ArcFlow may amplify errors or unintended incentives in a specified reward function; improved optimization does not by itself provide safety guarantees. Applying the method to physical or safety-critical systems would therefore require independently validated objectives, operational constraints, monitoring, and fail-safe mechanisms. We report task-level outcomes and the limits of the present evaluation to support accurate interpretation of the results.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: Code and artifacts are available in the anonymous repository at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/arcflow-868A . The repository contains the ArcFlow implementation, experiment configurations. The main text and appendices specify the algorithms, solver budgets, checkpoint-selection rule, evaluation conventions, and matched five-seed manipulation protocol; the repository provides the experiment configurations.

sections.heading: Empirical scope.
sections.text: Our evidence is limited to simulated control. The common-stack study covers DM Control, simulated Panda manipulation, and locomotion tasks, while the native image-policy study examines one manipulation task. These experiments do not establish robustness to real-robot sensing and actuation, safety constraints, distribution shift, or substantially larger policy and action spaces. The native study also implements the deployment-budget principle with endpoint supervision rather than the bridge objective, so it supports transfer of the principle but is not an independent test of the same update rule.

sections.heading: Comparison and statistical scope.
sections.text: Most baselines in the common-stack benchmark are controlled adaptations to a shared flow backbone, critic, and interaction budget; they are not reproductions of each method’s native architecture, pretraining, or published benchmark.

sections.heading: Training and selection cost.
sections.text: ArcFlow leaves deployment architecture and per-step solver cost unchanged, but training is not free: the bridge realization evaluates cached probes, cycles through several rollout budgets, and repeatedly measures validation return at K ∈ { 1 , 4 , 16 } K\in\{1,4,16\} . In the reported control protocol, validation adds 2.75 % 2.75\% to the environment-interaction count, in addition to neural-network compute from the probes and multi-budget evaluations. Moreover, selection protects only the budgets it evaluates and gives no guarantee for unseen solver counts.

sections.heading: Objective and theory.
sections.text: The bridge weight is an energy-based surrogate, not the likelihood ratio of the executed policy, and PPO-style clipping therefore has no exact trust-region interpretation. The appendix bounds finite-solver reconstruction error for a deterministic Euler field under Lipschitz assumptions; it does not prove monotone improvement in environment return, and it does not directly cover the clipped ShortCut operator used in the native pipeline. The fixed four-node bridge, the chosen budget sets, and the associated thresholds are empirical design choices. Whether the same choices remain effective with adaptive or higher-order solvers, continuous budget ranges, longer horizons, or other generative-policy parameterizations remains open.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY-SA 4.0 arXiv:2610.28788v1 [cs.LG] 20 Oct 2026 ArcFlow : Training Flow Policies for Multiple Solver Budgets Hieu Tran Email: hieutran@umass.edu Hong Yu Affiliation: University of Massachusetts Amherst University of Massachusetts Lowell Abstract Flow-matching policies adjust inference cost through the number of solver steps, but reinforcement learning at a single fixed solver budget can hide degradation at cheaper deployment budgets and even erase useful one-step behavior present in a pretrained policy. We introduce Action–Ratio–Clip Flow ( ArcFlow ) , a deployment-aware algorithm for training one flow policy across a specified range of solver budgets. ArcFlow combines action-aligned supervision, budget exposure, and worst-budget checkpoint selection. For reconstruction objectives, its bridge aggregates temporal probes into one surrogate ratio and one PPO-style clip per action, with a boundary residual exactly equal to deployed one-step reconstruction error. Cycling exposes the shared field to the deployment range, and selection optimizes its performance floor. For native velocity objectives, multi-budget endpoint supervision applies the same principle without replacing the native update. Both realizations preserve the architecture and deployment-time cost. Across DM Control, manipulation, and locomotion, ArcFlow attains the highest mean one-step return among five flow-policy baselines on 25 of 30 tasks under each method’s reported training settings. Component studies identify complementary improvements from boundary supervision, the fixed-grid bridge, budget exposure, and deployment selection. These results establish deployment-budget-aware training as an effective route to strong low-step control with one policy serving multiple inference costs. 1 1 1 Code can be accessed at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/arcflow-868A 1 Introduction Flow matching represents expressive action distributions by learning a velocity field that transports noise to actions ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . Its solver controls inference cost: more steps refine integration, while fewer steps reduce network evaluations, helping robotic policies meet latency budgets. Consistency and shortcut models enable one- and few-step generation ( Song et al., 2023 ; Frans et al., 2025 ) , creating an opportunity to retain expressive policies at low deployment cost. Reinforcement learning (RL) improves policies through interaction. FPO and FPO++ derive policy-gradient surrogates from flow-matching losses ( McAllister et al., 2025 ; Yi et al., 2026 ) ; Diffusion Policy Policy Optimization (DPPO) applies policy gradients to a stochastic diffusion denoising chain ( Ren et al., 2025 ) ; ReinFlow adds learnable exploration noise to flow policies ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) ; and PolicyFlow approximates importance ratios from velocity-field changes along interpolation paths ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . At deployment, solver steps determine latency and may change the action of the same trained field. High return at the training budget gives no assurance of high one-step return; RL can even erode low-step behavior already present in the prior. This gap motivates us to train and select one field across its deployment range (Figure 1 ). Figure 1: ArcFlow for multi-budget deployment. Left: the solver budget K K controls deployment cost. Right: the bridge-based control realization uses fresh noise and the observed action; at the boundary, the residual norm equals one-step reconstruction error. Probes are averaged before one surrogate ratio and PPO clip per action. Rollout budgets cycle, and checkpoint selection maximizes the worst validation return over K ∈ { 1 , 4 , 16 } K\in\{1,4,16\} . Two properties of the training objective and solver discretization help explain this behavior. First, reconstruction-based objectives may provide limited supervision at the deployment boundary. In FPO ( McAllister et al., 2025 ) , for example, the noise-reconstruction formulation weights velocity error by ( 1 − t ) 2 (1-t)^{2} , so the boundary queried by a one-step solver receives zero weight. Direct velocity supervision instead provides a boundary-aligned signal. This observation complements prior work on time-dependent loss weighting in generative modeling ( Choi et al., 2022 ; Hang et al., 2023 ) and highlights the importance of aligning the weighting scheme with the deployed action map. Second, because different solver budgets induce different action maps, updates based on rollouts from a single budget need not improve all budgets uniformly. We study this effect in the ReinFlow ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) fine-tuning pipeline, where native velocity supervision is already available. We introduce Action–Ratio–Clip Flow ( ArcFlow ) , an RL algorithm for one flow field across a specified solver-budget range. Its control realization uses a fixed-grid bridge with an exact one-step action-reconstruction residual. It aggregates temporal probes into one energy-based surrogate ratio and one PPO-style clip per action; the ratio is not the executed policy’s likelihood ratio. For native velocity objectives, multi-budget endpoint losses and an anchored max–min update extend the same deployment principle without replacing the original objective. Both realizations retain one field and the original deployment architecture. Our contributions are: • A diagnosis tied to deployment. We expose one-step degradation hidden by training-budget evaluation and identify how the supervision target suppresses the relevant boundary signal. • An algorithm for multiple solver budgets. We connect an exact action-reconstruction identity to action-aligned supervision, budget exposure, and worst-budget checkpoint selection. • Evidence across objectives and domains. A controlled common-stack benchmark and a released manipulation pipeline test the algorithm, with component studies and deployment-cost accounting identifying the sources of improvement. Across DM Control, manipulation, and locomotion, ArcFlow leads five flow-policy baselines in mean one-step return on 25 of 30 tasks including cross-regime manipulation comparisons. 2 Problem formulation Let s s denote an environment state, z ∼ p 0 z\sim p_{0} source noise, and v θ ​ ( x , t ∣ s ) v_{\theta}(x,t\mid s) a velocity field with reverse-time convention t : 1 → 0 t:1\to 0 . Our objective is to learn one field that remains useful across a specified set of deployment budgets, without supplying K K as an input to the field. Flow-policy algorithms use several tractable training signals, including flow-matching residuals, velocity-based surrogates, and likelihoods of stochastic internal transitions. These signals differ in their treatment of solver time. An improvement in a training surrogate, or in J K train J_{K_{\rm train}} , does not in itself imply an improvement in J K J_{K} for a different budget. We distinguish three outcomes. Numerical failure is a non-finite update or evaluation. Cross-budget degradation is a lower return at one deployment budget than another. Diffusion models learn reverse transport from noise to data ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ) , while deterministic samplers and neural ODEs expose an accuracy–computation tradeoff ( Song et al., 2021a ; Chen et al., 2018 ) . Flow matching and rectified flow learn velocity fields directly ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) ; transport couplings and multisample matching straighten paths, and rectified flows scale to high-resolution generation ( Tong et al., 2024 ; Pooladian et al., 2023 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . In control, generative models support planning and return conditioning ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Ajay et al., 2023 ) , plus visuomotor imitation across 2D, goal-conditioned, and 3D inputs ( Chi et al., 2023 ; Reuss et al., 2023 ; Ze et al., 2024 ) . AdaFlow adapts integration to action variance and FlowPolicy learns one-step consistency ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . This work instead trains one flow field with RL for a declared set of deployment budgets. Reinforcement learning of generative policies. Trust-region and clipped policy objectives motivate many modern policy updates ( Schulman et al., 2015 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ) . DDPO casts denoising as an MDP, while DRaFT differentiates rewards through the sampler ( Black et al., 2024 ; Clark et al., 2024 ) . For control, DPPO applies policy gradients to diffusion-policy denoising transitions and QVPO uses a value-weighted update ( Ren et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2024 ) . ReinFlow makes flow transitions stochastic; FPO and FPO++ form PPO-style ratios from flow losses; PolicyFlow and Flow-GRPO derive velocity- or transition-based objectives ( Zhang et al., 2025b ; McAllister et al., 2025 ; Yi et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . Offline and critic-based methods include Diffusion-QL, EDP, DTQL, BDPO, Q-score matching, Flow Q-Learning, and SAC Flow ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Kang et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Psenka et al., 2024 ; Park et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . ArcFlow focuses on the return floor of one policy across solver budgets. Few-step and one-step policies. DDIM and DPM-Solver accelerate sampling numerically ( Song et al., 2021a ; Lu et al., 2022 ) ; progressive distillation, consistency models, and InstaFlow learn fast generators ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . Shortcut models and MeanFlow train directly over variable or one-step generation ( Frans et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) , and Consistency Policy distills a visuomotor policy ( Prasad et al., 2024 ) . One-step flow policy mirror descent, FLAME, and MFPO bring this objective to RL ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026 ) . These methods optimize a designated short sampler or fast policy; ArcFlow preserves one RL-trained field and measures it at every declared K ∈ 𝒦 K\in\mathcal{K} . Training-time weighting and deployment budgets. P2, Min-SNR, and EDM reweight diffusion times ( Choi et al., 2022 ; Hang et al., 2023 ; Karras et al., 2022 ) . Our problematic weight instead follows algebraically from noise reconstruction and is zero at the one-step boundary. Boundary supervision restores that signal, solver cycling exposes the intended budgets, and worst-budget selection makes their return floor an explicit selection criterion. 7 Conclusion ArcFlow aligns flow-policy learning with its deployment range through boundary supervision, solver-budget exposure, and worst-budget selection. Across three control domains it improves one-step performance while retaining competitive higher-budget returns; the native ReinFlow study extends the principle to a released image-policy pipeline and five budgets. Deployment retains one architecture and pays only for the selected solver budget. Component studies further separate the gains from action-aligned supervision, budget exposure, and selection. These results support training and evaluating generative policies over their full deployment range. Generative AI was not used to generate or clean experimental datasets or to translate source material; qualitative or thematic data analysis was not applicable. We reviewed the AI-assisted work and take responsibility for the final text, claims, code, and artifacts. Ethics statement This work studies reinforcement learning for simulated control and does not involve human participants, personal data, or physical-robot experiments. Like other reinforcement-learning methods, ArcFlow may amplify errors or unintended incentives in a specified reward function; improved optimization does not by itself provide safety guarantees. Applying the method to physical or safety-critical systems would therefore require independently validated objectives, operational constraints, monitoring, and fail-safe mechanisms. We report task-level outcomes and the limits of the present evaluation to support accurate interpretation of the results. Reproducibility statement Code and artifacts are available in the anonymous repository at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/arcflow-868A . The repository contains the ArcFlow implementation, experiment configurations. The main text and appendices specify the algorithms, solver budgets, checkpoint-selection rule, evaluation conventions, and matched five-seed manipulation protocol; the repository provides the experiment configurations.
